title: The Beatitudes and the Fulfillment of the Law
summary: Jesus goes up on the mountain and begins the Sermon on the Mount, the first of Matthew's five great discourses, by pronouncing blessed the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, the hungry for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and the persecuted. He calls his disciples salt and light, says he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them, and in six sayings (‘you have heard that it was said, but I tell you’) presses the law on murder, adultery, divorce, oaths, retaliation, and love of neighbor down to the heart, ending with the call to be perfect as the Father is perfect.
story:
Chapter 4 ended with crowds streaming to Jesus from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan. Seeing them, he goes up on the mountain and sits down, the posture of a teacher, and his disciples come to him while the crowds listen (7:28-29). Readers who know Israel's story will think of Moses, who went up the mountain and brought God's law to the people. Jesus has just relived Israel's passage through the water and its testing in the wilderness, and now on a mountain he gives the charter of life in the kingdom he has begun to announce. Matthew never says that Jesus is a new Moses, but he arranges the scene so that the comparison cannot be missed, and then shows that the one who speaks is greater than Moses, since he says ‘I tell you’ where the prophets said ‘thus says the LORD’.

Chapters 5 to 7 are the first of five long discourses in Matthew, each closed by a formula like ‘when Jesus had finished saying these things’ (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). This chapter lays the foundation of the first discourse: who is blessed in God's kingdom, what the disciples are for in the world, how Jesus relates to the law of Moses, and what the greater righteousness looks like in anger, desire, marriage, speech, injury, and enmity. Chapter 6 will turn to the life of devotion before the Father, and chapter 7 will close with warnings and the call to build on Jesus' words.
historical:
The sermon is set in Galilee early in Jesus' ministry, in the late 20s AD, under the rule of Herod Antipas. Matthew does not name the mountain. Pilgrim tradition from the Byzantine period placed the teaching on the slopes above Tabgha, near Capernaum on the northwest shore of the lake, where remains of a small fourth-century church have been found; the present Church of the Beatitudes, an octagon whose eight sides recall the eight beatitudes, was built between 1936 and 1938 to a design by Antonio Barluzzi. Luke's parallel, the Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6:17-49), is set on a level place after Jesus comes down from a mountain and is about a third as long. Many scholars think Matthew and Luke drew on a common body of sayings and each arranged it for his readers; others think Luke knew Matthew; harmonizers since Augustine have noted that a traveling teacher would give similar teaching more than once. Matthew's sermon gathers sayings that Luke places in several settings (the Lord's Prayer in Luke 11, the lilies and ravens in Luke 12), which suggests that Matthew has composed a discourse from Jesus' teaching as a deliberate, ordered whole.

The chapter speaks into live debates of the Second Temple period. Scribes were the trained interpreters of the law, and the Pharisees were a lay movement known, according to Josephus, for handing on traditions of the fathers not written in the law of Moses (Antiquities 13.297); both were respected for their piety, which is why the demand for a greater righteousness (verse 20) would have startled Jesus' hearers. The sayings on divorce, oaths, and enemies each touch known positions. The Mishnah records the dispute between the schools of Shammai and Hillel over Deuteronomy 24:1, the first allowing divorce only for sexual unchastity and the second for almost any cause, with Rabbi Akiva adding even that the husband found another woman more beautiful (m. Gittin 9:10). The Damascus Document from Qumran condemns taking a second wife while the first lives, citing ‘male and female he created them’ (CD 4:20-21), the text Jesus himself cites in 19:4. On oaths, Sirach had warned against making a habit of swearing (Sirach 23:9-11), and Josephus says the Essenes avoided oaths altogether, regarding them as worse than perjury, since one who cannot be believed without calling on God is already condemned (Jewish War 2.135). On enemies, the Community Rule from Qumran tells its members to love all the sons of light and hate all the sons of darkness (1QS 1:9-10), the closest known parallel to the saying Jesus quotes in verse 43.

Beatitudes as a form were at home in Jewish wisdom. A fragmentary Hebrew text from Qumran Cave 4, known as 4Q525 or 4QBeatitudes and first published in full by Émile Puech in 1991, contains a series of short blessings in the form ‘Blessed is the one who…’ followed by a longer final one, all praising the one who seeks wisdom and keeps the law. The War Scroll speaks of the ‘poor in spirit’ among the faithful in the final battle (1QM 14:7). Jesus' beatitudes share the form but not the content: they bless people not for achieved wisdom but for their need, their grief, and their longing, and promise them the kingdom.

Roman rule lies behind several sayings. The court and the prison of verses 25 and 26, with a jailer who holds a debtor until the last quadrans is paid, reflect Greek and Roman practice more than Jewish law. The command to go a second mile (verse 41) uses angareuō, a Persian loanword for official requisition; Roman soldiers and officials could compel civilians to carry baggage or supply animals for transport, and the verb reappears when soldiers compel Simon of Cyrene to carry Jesus' cross (27:32). In a land where such demands were common and resented, the saying was pointed.
cultural:
A beatitude (from the Latin beatus, ‘blessed’) is a declaration that someone is fortunate or in a good condition before God. The Psalms open with one, “Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked” (Psalm 1:1), and the Hebrew ashrei behind it is a congratulation, not a wish. Jesus pronounces blessed the people his culture would have pitied or overlooked. The poor and the humble (anavim) had long been called God's people in the Psalms and prophets, those with no protector but him (Psalm 37:11, Isaiah 61:1-3), and the first four beatitudes echo those texts. Mourning was public and ritualized in the ancient world, with professional mourners, torn garments, and seven days of lamentation for the dead, and in Isaiah 61:3 the mourners are those who grieve over Zion's ruin; Jesus promises them the comfort Isaiah promised.

Honor and shame governed social life in Galilee, as across the Mediterranean world. Public insult was a serious injury; the Babylonian Talmud says that one who shames a neighbor in public, making his face go white, is like one who sheds blood (b. Bava Metzia 58b), and the Mishnah fixes a heavier penalty for a slap with the back of the hand, the gesture of contempt, than for an ordinary blow (m. Bava Qamma 8:6). That background explains why Jesus places the insults ‘Raca’ (an Aramaic word meaning roughly ‘empty-head’) and ‘fool’ beside murder, and why a blow to the right cheek, which from a right-handed striker would be backhanded, is an insult to honor more than an assault. Reconciliation was a matter of restoring honor between persons, and the Mishnah teaches that the Day of Atonement does not atone for wrongs between a person and a neighbor until the neighbor has been appeased (m. Yoma 8:9), a close parallel to verses 23 and 24.

Marriage and divorce worked differently from modern law. In Jewish practice the husband alone could initiate a divorce by giving his wife a written bill (get), which Deuteronomy 24:1 required and which protected her by proving she was free to remarry. Josephus remarks that when Herod's sister Salome sent her husband Costobarus a bill of divorce, she acted contrary to Jewish law, which allowed only the husband to do so (Antiquities 15.259-260). A divorced woman without a family to return to usually needed to remarry to survive, which is why Jesus says the husband who divorces her ‘makes her commit adultery’ (verse 32): the responsibility for what follows falls on him. Greek and Roman law allowed either spouse to divorce, and Mark's version of the saying addresses a wife who divorces her husband as well (Mark 10:12).

Oaths were woven into daily speech. People swore by heaven, by earth, by Jerusalem, by the temple, or by their own heads, and debated which formulas were binding: the Mishnah rules that one who adjures by heaven and earth is not liable (m. Shevuot 4:13), and Jesus condemns similar distinctions in 23:16-22. The underlying problem was a double standard of truth, careful when God's name was invoked and careless otherwise. Salt in verse 13 was the preservative and seasoning of every kitchen; the salt gathered around the Dead Sea was mixed with other minerals and could leach away when damp, leaving a useless residue. The lamp of verse 15 was a small clay oil lamp, and the ‘basket’ (modios) a grain measure of about nine liters that could be set over it. Gehenna (verses 22, 29, 30) was the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, where children had been burned in sacrifice at Topheth (Jeremiah 7:31), and by Jesus' day its name had become the common Jewish term for the place of final judgment. The greeting of verse 47 was the greeting of peace, shalom, which carried a blessing and was often withheld from outsiders; tax collectors were local agents who bought the right to collect tolls and were despised as collaborators and cheats.
literary:
The Sermon on the Mount is framed by a narrative introduction (5:1-2) and conclusion (7:28-29), and its body is bracketed by two references to ‘the Law and the Prophets’ (5:17 and 7:12), which mark 5:17 to 7:12 as the instruction on the greater righteousness, with the beatitudes and images of salt and light as its prelude and the warnings of 7:13-27 as its close. This chapter has three parts. The beatitudes (verses 3 to 12) are eight balanced sayings in the third person, the first and eighth ending with the same promise, ‘theirs is the kingdom of heaven’, an inclusio that frames the whole; the ninth turns to the second person, ‘Blessed are you’, and applies the blessings to the listeners. The first four beatitudes each begin, after makarioi, with a word starting with the letter p in Greek (ptōchoi, penthountes, praeis, peinōntes), and the first half concerns need, the second half conduct. Righteousness closes each half (verses 6 and 10).

The second part (verses 13 to 20) turns from ‘they’ to an emphatic ‘you’: ‘You are the salt of the earth’ and ‘You are the light of the world.’ It then states the thesis of the sermon: Jesus has come not to abolish but to fulfill the Law and the Prophets, the law stands until all is accomplished, and the disciples' righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees. The third part (verses 21 to 48) gives six sayings, each introduced by some form of ‘you have heard that it was said’ and continued with ‘but I tell you’. The first and fourth have the fuller formula ‘it was said to the ancients’, and the fourth begins with ‘again’, which divides the six into two groups of three. Christian scholarship has called them the ‘antitheses’, but the name can mislead: in most of them Jesus does not contradict the command but goes beneath or beyond it. Amy-Jill Levine calls them ‘extensions’, and Glen Stassen (Journal of Biblical Literature 122, 2003) argued that each section has three parts, a traditional teaching, a diagnosis of the vicious cycle behind it, and a ‘transforming initiative’ such as going to be reconciled or going the second mile.

The six sayings draw on different parts of the law. The first two quote the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:13-14); the third summarizes Deuteronomy 24:1; the fourth paraphrases Leviticus 19:12, Numbers 30:2, and Deuteronomy 23:21; the fifth quotes the rule of proportionate penalty (Exodus 21:24); and the sixth quotes Leviticus 19:18 alongside a line that is not in the law at all. The chapter closes with a summary that echoes both Leviticus 19:2, “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy”, and Deuteronomy 18:13, where the Septuagint's ‘you shall be perfect’ (teleios esē) renders the Hebrew call to be blameless. The word ‘more’ (perisson) links verse 20 with verse 47, so the ‘more’ of the greater righteousness is finally defined as love that goes beyond reciprocity. Throughout, Jesus uses vivid overstatement (tear out the eye, cut off the hand) and concrete cases (the altar, the courtroom, the mile) rather than abstract rules, the manner of a prophet and a wisdom teacher rather than a legislator.

outline.t: Jesus sits on the mountain to teach
The Beatitudes
Salt of the earth and light of the world
Jesus fulfills the Law and the Prophets
On anger and reconciliation
On lust
On divorce
On oaths
On retaliation
On love for enemies

doctrines.note: The beatitudes describe the people of the kingdom and promise them its gifts: comfort, the earth, fullness, mercy, the sight of God, the name of sons. The first and last promises are in the present tense (‘theirs is the kingdom’) and the rest in the future, so the kingdom is both given now and awaited. It reverses the world's judgment about who is fortunate, and it belongs to those who know their need.

Jesus did not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them (verse 17). He affirms the law's lasting authority, interprets it with his own ‘I tell you’, presses its commands down to the heart, and brings it to the goal it pointed toward. Christians differ over how the law of Moses applies to believers now: Lutheran, Reformed, Anabaptist, Catholic, and other traditions describe its continuing uses differently, but all read this chapter as a call to the righteousness the law intended.

The chapter climbs to the command to love enemies and pray for persecutors (verse 44), grounded in the Father's generosity to the evil and the good. Love here is action: reconciling before worship, refusing revenge, giving, going the second mile, greeting outsiders. Christians have disagreed about whether these commands forbid all use of force, with the peace churches holding that they do and the just war tradition holding that they govern personal response but not the state's duty to protect; both agree that they forbid hatred and revenge.

‘Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect’ (verse 48) echoes the call of Leviticus to be holy as God is holy. Teleios means whole, complete, undivided, and in context it describes a love that does not stop at friends. Holiness is not separation from enemies but likeness to a Father who sends sun and rain on all.

Jesus treats marriage as a covenant not to be dissolved at will. Against the practice that let a husband dismiss his wife with a certificate, he holds the husband responsible for the harm divorce does, allowing an exception for sexual immorality (verse 32). He also guards marriage at the level of desire (verses 27 and 28). How the exception applies has long divided Christian traditions.

words.note: Makarios, blessed, fortunate, happy. It occurs about fifty times in the New Testament, thirteen in Matthew and nine in this chapter. In the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew ashrei, as in Psalm 1:1, a declaration of someone's good standing, not a wish or a mood. BDAG glosses it as privileged recipient of divine favor. It is distinct from eulogētos, ‘blessed’ in the sense of praised, used of God. Jonathan Pennington (The Sermon on the Mount and Human Flourishing, 2017) argues that it names true human flourishing. Jesus does not command people to become poor or grieving to earn blessing; he announces what God's kingdom means for those who are.

Ptōchos, poor, destitute, one who must beg. It occurs about thirty-four times in the New Testament, five in Matthew and ten in Luke. Greek distinguished the ptōchos from the penēs, who worked and had little. In the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew words for the afflicted poor who look to God (Isaiah 61:1). Matthew's ‘poor in spirit’ and Luke's ‘you who are poor’ (Luke 6:20) have often been set against each other, but in the Psalms and Isaiah economic poverty and humble dependence on God already overlap, and the War Scroll's ‘poor in spirit’ (1QM 14:7) describes the humble faithful.

Praus, gentle, meek, humble. It occurs only four times in the New Testament: here, twice more in Matthew of Jesus himself (11:29, 21:5, quoting Zechariah 9:9), and in 1 Peter 3:4. In the Septuagint it renders anav, the humble, in Psalm 37:11, which verse 5 quotes almost word for word. Meekness in this sense is not weakness but a refusal to grasp or retaliate, entrusting one's cause to God; Moses is called the most humble man on earth (Numbers 12:3).

Dikaiosynē, righteousness, justice. It occurs about ninety-two times in the New Testament, thirty-four in Romans and seven in Matthew (3:15; 5:6, 10, 20; 6:1, 33; 21:32). Protestant readers following Luther have often heard Paul's sense of a righteousness God gives; most recent Matthew scholars, including Benno Przybylski (1980) and Ulrich Luz, argue that in Matthew it means conduct that conforms to God's will, while others hear in verse 6 a longing for God's justice to be set right in the world. The greater righteousness of verse 20 is the disciples' own way of life, which the rest of the chapter describes.

Plēroō, to fill, complete, fulfill. It occurs about eighty-six times in the New Testament and sixteen in Matthew, most often in the formula ‘to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet’ (1:22, 2:15, 4:14). Interpreters debate its sense in verse 17: that Jesus obeys the law perfectly, that he teaches its full meaning, or that he brings the Law and the Prophets to the goal they pointed toward. Matthew's usage elsewhere favors the last, and Davies and Allison (International Critical Commentary, 1988) hold the senses together. The opposite, katalyō, is ‘tear down’, the verb used for destroying the temple (24:2, 26:61).

Geenna, Gehenna, from the Hebrew ge hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom. It occurs twelve times in the New Testament, seven in Matthew, three in this chapter, and all but one (James 3:6) on Jesus' lips. The valley was the site of child sacrifice under Ahaz and Manasseh (2 Kings 23:10, Jeremiah 7:31-32), and by the first century its name had become a term for the place of final judgment, as in 1 Enoch 27 and later rabbinic texts. Christians differ on how to understand the nature and duration of that judgment, but Jesus uses the word to show that contempt and lust are matters of ultimate weight.

Porneia, sexual immorality. It occurs about twenty-five times in the New Testament, three in Matthew (5:32, 15:19, 19:9). It is a broad word covering many kinds of sexual sin: prostitution, fornication, adultery, and incestuous or otherwise unlawful unions (Acts 15:20, 1 Corinthians 5:1). Its breadth is why the exception in verse 32 is disputed. Some take it as adultery within marriage, some as unfaithfulness during betrothal, and some as marriages within forbidden degrees of kinship (Leviticus 18), a reading Joseph Fitzmyer supported from the Dead Sea Scrolls (Theological Studies, 1976).

Teleios, complete, whole, mature, perfect. It occurs about nineteen times in the New Testament, three in Matthew (twice in 5:48 and in 19:21, ‘If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions’). In the Septuagint it renders Hebrew tamim, ‘whole, blameless’, used of Noah (Genesis 6:9) and required of Israel before God (Deuteronomy 18:13). It does not mean flawless performance so much as undivided wholeness of heart toward God. Luke's parallel reads, ‘Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful’ (Luke 6:36).

christ:
The chapter reveals Jesus' authority above all. Moses received the law and delivered it; the prophets introduced God's word with ‘thus says the LORD’. Jesus says, six times, ‘But I tell you’, and prefaces his claim about the law with ‘Amen I tell you’ (verse 18), vouching for his own word. When the sermon ends, the crowds are astonished because “He taught as one who had authority, and not as their scribes” (7:29). In verse 11 he blesses those persecuted ‘because of Me’, treating loyalty to himself as equivalent to the loyalty to righteousness in verse 10, a claim the Scriptures reserved for loyalty to God. He also claims to have ‘come’ (verse 17), language that implies he was sent and has a mission from beyond.

He claims to fulfill the Law and the Prophets, and the rest of Matthew shows how: by teaching their true intent, by his own obedience, and by his death and resurrection, when he pours out ‘My blood of the covenant’ for the forgiveness of sins (26:28) and receives all authority (28:18). The beatitudes are, at the same time, a portrait of Jesus himself. He is ‘gentle and humble in heart’ (11:29), using the word of verse 5; he comes to Jerusalem meek (21:5); he mourns over the city (23:37); he shows mercy to the sick and sinners; he is persecuted for righteousness and reviled falsely at his trial. The commands of the second half of the chapter are the life he lived: he does not resist the evil man who strikes him (26:67), fulfilling the servant's words, “I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard” (Isaiah 50:6); he answers with truth rather than oaths before the high priest (26:63-64); and he prays for his enemies, for according to Luke he said on the cross, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

The Father of verse 45, who sends sun and rain on the evil and the good, is the Father whom Jesus makes known, and those who love as he loves ‘may be sons of your Father in heaven’. The sonship tested in chapter 4 is now shared: disciples become children of the Father by being joined to the Son and reflecting the Father's generosity. The chapter therefore presents Jesus not only as a teacher of a higher ethic but as the one in whom that ethic is embodied and through whom people are brought into the Father's family, where the call to be ‘perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect’ becomes a promise as well as a command.
interpretation:
The earliest Christian writings already quote these sayings: the Didache (1:3-5) repeats the commands to pray for enemies and give to all who ask, and Justin Martyr (First Apology 15-16, around 155) set them before the emperor as the Christian way of life. Augustine's commentary De sermone Domini in monte (written about 393 to 396, while he was a priest at Hippo), whose Latin title gave the passage its familiar name, called it the perfect pattern of the Christian life and linked the beatitudes to the seven gifts of the Spirit in Isaiah 11 and to the petitions of the Lord's Prayer. John Chrysostom preached through it in his homilies on Matthew (around 390), and Gregory of Nyssa's eight homilies on the Beatitudes read them as steps of the soul's ascent to God. Thomas Aquinas, following Augustine, held that the sermon contains the whole formation of the Christian life (Summa Theologiae I-II, question 108, article 3), and distinguished the precepts binding on all from the counsels of poverty, chastity, and obedience that religious take up by vow (article 4). Protestants have often described this as reserving the sermon for monks; classical Catholic teaching held its commands binding on every Christian, and the Second Vatican Council, citing verse 48, taught that all the faithful are called to the perfection of charity (Lumen Gentium 40, 1964).

The Reformation divided over the sermon's scope. Luther's weekly sermons on Matthew 5 to 7 (preached from 1530, published 1532) distinguished the Christian as a person, who must suffer wrong without revenge, from the Christian in an office such as judge or soldier, who serves the neighbor by bearing the sword; Calvin's Harmony of the Gospels (1555) read the oath and cheek sayings similarly. The Anabaptist Schleitheim Confession (1527) took the sermon as binding church order, declaring the sword ordained by God outside the perfection of Christ and forbidding oaths (articles 6 and 7), and Mennonites and later the Quakers, in their declaration to Charles II in 1660, made refusal of war a public testimony. The just war tradition, from Augustine (Against Faustus 22.74) to Aquinas (Summa II-II, question 40), held that love of neighbor can require the protection of the innocent by legitimate authority, while the early pacifist voices of Tertullian (On Idolatry 19) and Origen (Against Celsus 8.73) were revived by the peace churches.

Modern readings multiplied. Leo Tolstoy (What I Believe, 1884) drew five commandments from verses 21 to 48 and read ‘resist not evil’ as forbidding all force. Albert Schweitzer called the sermon an interim ethic for the short time before an expected end. The Scofield Reference Bible (1909) taught that the sermon is in its primary application the law of the coming kingdom, with a moral application to the church; later dispensationalists apply it directly to believers. Dietrich Bonhoeffer's Discipleship (1937) insisted that its commands are meant to be obeyed by those who follow Christ, and Reinhold Niebuhr (An Interpretation of Christian Ethics, 1935) called its love an impossible possibility. Jewish scholars have engaged it closely: Joseph Klausner (Jesus of Nazareth, 1922) judged its ethic Jewish but impractically extreme, Claude Montefiore (Rabbinic Literature and Gospel Teachings, 1930) gathered rabbinic parallels, Pinchas Lapide wrote The Sermon on the Mount: Utopia or Program for Action? (English 1986), and Jacob Neusner, in A Rabbi Talks with Jesus (1993), explained respectfully why, hearing it, he would have remained with the Torah of Moses.

Matthew 5:1-12 is the Gospel for All Saints' Day in Year A of the Revised Common Lectionary, which reads the rest of the chapter on the fourth to seventh Sundays after the Epiphany. In the Byzantine Divine Liturgy the Beatitudes are sung on Sundays as the third antiphon with the thief's plea, ‘Remember us, O Lord, when you come into your kingdom.’ Fra Angelico painted the sermon in a cell at San Marco in Florence (1440s), Cosimo Rosselli on the wall of the Sistine Chapel (1481 to 1482), and Arvo Pärt set the Beatitudes for choir and organ (1990).
text:
Several verses read differently in older and newer English Bibles because of the manuscripts. In verse 22 most later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, say that whoever is angry with his brother ‘without a cause’ (eikē) is liable to judgment; the word is absent from Codex Sinaiticus in its first hand, Codex Vaticanus, and probably the early papyrus P64, and Jerome noted that the better copies lacked it. Most editors regard it as a scribal softening. In verse 44 the King James Version has a longer command, ‘bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you’, filled out from Luke 6:27-28; Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and early versions have only ‘love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you’. In verse 47 later manuscripts repeat ‘tax collectors’ where the earlier have ‘Gentiles’. In verse 27 the later manuscripts add ‘to the ancients’ (KJV ‘by them of old time’) to match verses 21 and 33. Codex Bezae and some Latin and Syriac witnesses place the mourners' beatitude after the meek (verses 4 and 5 reversed), and a few witnesses lack ‘falsely’ in verse 11 and the last clause of verse 32; modern editions keep the familiar order and include both.

Translation also shapes what readers see. The KJV's ‘by them of old time’ in verse 21 takes the dative as the speakers; modern versions render it ‘to the ancients’ or ‘to those of old’, the Sinai generation who heard the law. In verse 39 the KJV reads ‘resist not evil’, the neuter, while the BSB and most modern versions take the word as masculine, ‘an evil person’, which fits the examples that follow; the difference was central to Tolstoy's reading. ‘Hell fire’ (KJV) and ‘the fire of hell’ (BSB) both render ‘the Gehenna of fire’. The ‘jot’ and ‘tittle’ of verse 18 in the KJV are the iota and the keraia, the smallest letter and the smallest stroke. In verse 32 ‘except for sexual immorality’ (BSB, ESV) is ‘saving for the cause of fornication’ in the KJV and ‘unless the marriage is unlawful’ in the New American Bible Revised Edition, a rendering that reflects one of the interpretations described below. In verse 48 ‘perfect’ is traditional; some modern renderings prefer ‘complete’ or ‘whole’ to avoid suggesting flawlessness.

teach.big: Jesus, speaking with an authority greater than Moses, blesses the needy who belong to God's kingdom and calls them to a righteousness that fulfills the law from the heart and reaches even to love for enemies, reflecting the Father's own generosity.

outline.t: The Messiah teaches on the mountain as Israel's authoritative teacher, and his words are addressed to disciples within hearing of the crowd.
God's blessing rests on those who know their need and hunger for his justice; the kingdom reverses the world's verdict and turns persecution into the company of the prophets.
Disciples are already salt and light by Jesus' word; their calling is to be what they are, so that others see their deeds and glorify the Father, not them.
Jesus brings the Law and the Prophets to their goal rather than discarding them, and the righteousness of his people must exceed the most respected piety of the day.
Murder begins in contempt, and reconciliation with a wronged brother comes before worship; urgency, not delay, is the wise response to a broken relationship.
Adultery begins in the desire to possess, and disciples must deal decisively with whatever leads them into sin, since the whole person is at stake.
Marriage is not dissolved at a husband's convenience; Jesus holds the one who divorces responsible for the harm, while allowing an exception for sexual immorality.
Truthfulness should need no oath, because every word is spoken before God; a plain yes and no is the speech of the kingdom.
The law limited revenge; Jesus calls disciples to renounce it, answering insult, lawsuit, requisition, and need with generosity rather than retaliation.
Love reaches to enemies and persecutors because the Father's goodness reaches the evil and the good, and to be his children is to be whole in that love.

teach.pitfalls:
The most common misreading treats the beatitudes as entrance requirements, a ladder of virtues to climb in order to earn God's favor. They are announcements of grace to people who are poor, grieving, and hungry, and the kingdom is given before it is demanded. The opposite error spiritualizes them until they have nothing to do with real poverty or real grief. A third error makes the antitheses a contrast between a Jewish religion of outward rules and a Christian religion of the heart. Jesus quotes the Torah as God's word, the Torah itself commands love of neighbor and forbids coveting, and Jewish teachers made the same moves toward the heart (the Mishnah on reconciliation before the Day of Atonement, the rabbinic saying that adultery can be committed with the eyes in Leviticus Rabbah 23:12). The contrast in verse 20 is with a particular level of practice, not with Judaism.

On the hard commands, avoid both evasion and cruelty. Evasion reduces them to ideals no one is expected to keep, or assigns them only to monks, or only to a future kingdom; each tradition that has limited their scope has also insisted that they bind disciples now in some real way. Cruelty applies them mechanically in ways Jesus did not intend: telling an abused spouse that turning the other cheek means staying in danger, or using verse 32 to shame people whose marriages ended through no fault of their own. Jesus himself protested when struck unjustly (John 18:23). Verses 29 and 30 are hyperbole and must never be taught as a literal instruction. The call to be perfect in verse 48 is not a demand for flawless performance but for whole-hearted love, and it should not be preached in a way that drives the scrupulous to despair.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on many people in a room. The divorced and remarried, and those who have been abandoned or betrayed, may hear verse 32 as a verdict on them; teach what Jesus says about the one who divorces unjustly, name the range of Christian understanding, and make clear that the church's word is not legal advice and that people in marriages marked by violence or abuse should seek safety and help first. Victims of abuse need to hear that loving an enemy never requires remaining under violence. The sayings on lust and on tearing out an eye weigh heavily on the scrupulous and on people with obsessive thoughts; say plainly that the language is figurative, that intrusive unwanted thoughts are not the same as a willed look of possession, and that anyone having thoughts of harming themselves should speak to someone they trust or contact emergency or crisis services at once. The mourning and the persecuted should hear verse 4 as God's promise to them, not as a demand to feel blessed.

hard.q: Does Jesus set himself against the law of Moses in this chapter, or does he keep it?
hard.a:
The objection comes from opposite directions. Marcion of Sinope in the second century held that Jesus revealed a God opposed to the God of the law, and his work Antitheses set Old Testament and Gospel sayings against each other; Tertullian answered him at length (Against Marcion 4). Faustus the Manichean, whom Augustine answered in Against Faustus 17 to 19, argued that verse 17 could not be a genuine saying because Jesus plainly departed from the law. Many modern readers, Christian and not, have heard ‘You have heard… but I tell you’ as Jesus overriding Moses, especially on oaths and on eye for eye. Jewish readers have pressed the point from the other side. Jacob Neusner (A Rabbi Talks with Jesus, 1993) argued that by setting ‘I tell you’ over the Torah and making himself the center, Jesus claims an authority no faithful Israelite could grant a teacher, and that a Jew who heard him would rightly have stayed with Moses. Joseph Klausner (1922) found the ethic Jewish at its core but so extreme as to be impracticable for a nation.

Responses begin from verses 17 to 19, where Jesus denies coming to abolish the Law and the Prophets and says not a stroke will pass away. Most commentators, including W. D. Davies and Dale Allison (1988) and Ulrich Luz, read the six sayings as intensifying or radicalizing the law's intent rather than annulling it: no one who refrains from anger will murder, no one who refuses to swear will perjure himself, and no one who loves enemies will break the command to love the neighbor. Jewish scholars such as Pinchas Lapide (1986) and Amy-Jill Levine (2020) have read them in the same way as a Jewish teacher's ‘fence around the Torah’ (m. Avot 1:1), guarding a command by setting a stricter boundary around it, and have noted how closely rabbinic sayings run alongside them. The harder cases are divorce, oaths, and retaliation, where Jesus forbids what the law permitted or regulated. Here many interpreters argue that the law's permission was a concession, as Jesus says of divorce in 19:8, “Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart; but it was not this way from the beginning”, and that Jesus returns to the Creator's intention. Others, especially in the Lutheran and Reformed traditions, see in these sayings a claim that the Messiah has authority to interpret and fulfill the law as its Lord, so that the law is now read through him. Neusner's point stands in its own terms: the chapter's deepest claim is not about particular rules but about who Jesus is, and on that question Jews and Christians part with mutual understanding rather than agreement.

hard.q: What does Jesus teach about divorce and remarriage, and what does the exception ‘except for sexual immorality’ mean?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real and the stakes are personal. Mark 10:11-12, Luke 16:18, and Paul, who cites the Lord's command (1 Corinthians 7:10-11), give Jesus' teaching without any exception, while Matthew includes one here and in 19:9. Many historians, among them John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, volume 4, 2009), conclude that Jesus forbade divorce absolutely and that the exception reflects Matthew's application of his teaching in the church. Others object from the side of pastoral experience: a rule that binds a betrayed, deserted, or abused spouse to a marriage that has been destroyed seems to lay a burden on the innocent, and critics of the church have seen in its divorce teaching a source of real suffering, especially for women.

The traditions answer differently, and each has serious defenders. The earliest Christian discussion, the Shepherd of Hermas (Mandate 4.1, second century), taught that a husband should separate from an unrepentant adulterous wife but not remarry, leaving room for her repentance, and the Western church came to hold that a valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved; the Council of Trent (1563, session 24, canon 7) affirmed that even adultery does not dissolve the bond, while permitting separation, and Catholic practice also examines whether a true marriage existed at all (a declaration of nullity). Some Catholic and other scholars, with Joseph Fitzmyer (1976), read porneia as marriage within forbidden degrees of kinship, so that the exception concerns unions that were never lawful. The Orthodox churches hold marriage to be lifelong in principle but, by pastoral economy (oikonomia), permit a second and in some cases a third marriage after divorce, with a penitential rite.

Most Protestant traditions, following Erasmus's annotations of 1519 and the Reformers, hold that adultery breaks the marriage covenant and permits the innocent party to divorce and remarry; the Westminster Confession (1646, 24.5-6) allows divorce for adultery and for willful desertion that cannot be remedied, reading 1 Corinthians 7:15 beside this verse. Some evangelicals hold that the exception refers to unfaithfulness during betrothal, as when Joseph resolved to divorce Mary (1:19), so that no remarriage is permitted after a completed marriage; John Piper has argued this view. William Heth and Gordon Wenham (Jesus and Divorce, 1984) defended the early church's view of no remarriage, though Heth later changed his position. David Instone-Brewer (Divorce and Remarriage in the Bible, 2002) argued that Jesus was answering the Hillelite ‘any cause’ divorce (compare 19:3) and did not abolish the other biblical grounds, including neglect and abuse (Exodus 21:10-11), a view that has drawn both support and criticism. No position should be taught as if the question were settled among faithful Christians. What all share is Jesus' refusal to treat marriage as disposable and his protection of the one put away, and churches of every tradition now recognize that a person in danger must be helped to safety first.

observe: List the eight groups Jesus calls blessed in verses 3 to 10 and the promise attached to each. Which promises are present and which are future?
In each of the six sayings of verses 21 to 48, what did the hearers ‘hear’, and what does Jesus say in reply?
What reasons does Jesus give in verse 45 for loving enemies?
interpret: What does Jesus mean by fulfilling the Law and the Prophets, and how do verses 21 to 48 show what that fulfillment looks like?
Why does Jesus place contempt and lustful desire beside murder and adultery? What does that reveal about how God sees sin?
How would you explain ‘Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect’ in light of verses 43 to 47?
apply: Which beatitude most contradicts what your culture calls a good life, and which do you most need to hear as good news rather than as a demand?
Is there someone who has something against you whom you need to approach before you next come to worship?
Who is the enemy you find hardest to pray for, and what would it mean to pray for them this week?
